title: Processor Fundamentals + Parameter Passing
instructions: Answer all questions. Section A covers processor fundamentals, Section B covers parameter passing. Calculators are not permitted.

questions.text: What is the function of the **program counter (PC)**?

options.text: It stores the address of the next instruction to be fetched
It stores the instruction currently being executed
It stores the result of arithmetic operations
It counts the number of clock cycles

questions.explanation: PC holds the address of the next instruction; it is incremented after each fetch (unless a jump/branch changes it).

questions.text: Which bus carries control signals such as read/write and clock pulses?
questions.explanation: The control bus is bidirectional and carries signals such as memory read/write, interrupt requests and clock.

questions.text: Describe the role of the **control unit** and the **ALU** in the processor.

answer.text: Control unit: fetches and decodes instructions and generates the control signals that coordinate the other components.
ALU: performs arithmetic operations (add, subtract) and logical operations (AND, OR, NOT, comparisons/shifts) on data in registers.

questions.explanation: CU = 'director' of the CPU; ALU = 'calculator'. Two marks each require two clear functions.

questions.text: A processor has an address bus that is **24 bits** wide. How many memory locations can it address? Give your answer in **MiB** (use 1 Mi = 2²⁰).
The **clock speed** of a CPU is measured in which unit?
questions.explanation: Clock speed is the number of cycles per second — typically GHz. Higher clock speed usually means more instructions per second.

questions.text: Explain how **cache memory** improves processor performance.

answer.text: Cache is fast memory close to the CPU that stores frequently used instructions and data.
It reduces the need to access slower main memory (RAM), reducing average access time.
Because the FDE cycle can get data from cache much faster than from RAM, the CPU waits less and throughput increases.

questions.explanation: Levels: L1 (fastest, smallest, on-chip), L2, L3 (larger, slower).

questions.text: What is the purpose of **pipelining** in a processor?

options.text: To allow multiple instructions to be at different stages of the FDE cycle at the same time
To increase the size of the RAM
To compress the program before it is executed
To translate assembly language into machine code

questions.explanation: While one instruction is executed, the next is decoded and the one after is fetched — improving throughput (though branches can cause pipeline stalls).

questions.text: State **two** factors, other than clock speed, that affect the performance of a processor.

answer.text: Number of cores (more cores can process more instructions in parallel).
Size/type of cache and bus width (or word length) — affects how much data can be handled at once.

questions.explanation: Other valid: instruction set design (RISC/CISC), pipelining, amount of RAM installed.

questions.text: Explain, in order, what the **decode** and **execute** stages of the FDE cycle do.

answer.text: Decode: the control unit interprets the opcode/operand in the CIR and works out what operation is required.
Execute: the control unit sends signals to the relevant components; the ALU carries out the arithmetic/logic operation or data is moved.
The result is stored in a register (usually the accumulator), and the cycle repeats.

questions.explanation: The FDE order is: PC→MAR→memory→MDR→CIR, decode, then execute.

questions.text: Which is the **fastest** type of storage in a computer system?
questions.explanation: Order (fastest → slowest, smallest → largest): registers → L1 → L2 → L3 cache → RAM → SSD/HDD.

questions.text: Explain **how the scheduling of threads** on a multi-core processor speeds up a program such as video editing.

answer.text: A program can be split into multiple threads that each perform a separate part of the task.
The threads are distributed across different cores so tasks run in parallel rather than sequentially.
Each core can execute its thread at the same time as the others, so the total time is reduced.
The operating system schedules the threads and balances the load between the cores.

questions.explanation: Parallelism requires the task to be divisible into independent pieces; otherwise speed-up is limited.

questions.text: `PROCEDURE Double(BYREF N : INTEGER)` receives `X` where `X = 6`. The procedure executes `N ← N * 2`. What is the value of `X` afterwards?
questions.explanation: BYREF passes the address, so the change is made to the original variable X, which becomes 12.

questions.text: `PROCEDURE Change(BYVAL N : INTEGER)` receives `X` where `X = 6`, then executes `N ← 99`. What is the value of `X` afterwards?
questions.explanation: BYVAL sends a copy, so N becomes 99 but the original X is untouched.

questions.text: Explain, using an example, the difference between **passing by value** and **passing by reference**, including **one advantage of each**.

answer.text: By value: the subroutine receives a copy of the value; the original variable is not changed.
Advantage: the original data is protected (no side effects), which makes debugging easier.
By reference: the subroutine receives the address of the variable, so it can modify the original variable.
Advantage: allows more than one value to be 'returned' / avoids copying large data, so it is more memory efficient.

questions.explanation: Classic exam example: a Swap procedure must use BYREF, otherwise the original values are unchanged.

questions.text:
Trace the following code and complete the table.

```
DECLARE A : INTEGER
DECLARE B : INTEGER
A ← 10
B ← 20
CALL Update(A, B)
OUTPUT A, B

PROCEDURE Update(BYREF X : INTEGER, BYVAL Y : INTEGER)
    X ← X + 5
    Y ← Y + 5
    OUTPUT X, Y
ENDPROCEDURE
```
questions.explanation: X is by reference → A becomes 15. Y is by value → B stays 20 (only the copy is changed). Final output is '15 20'.

questions.text: Write a procedure `UpdateScore` that takes a score **by reference** and a bonus **by value**, adds the bonus to the score (to a maximum of 100), and does not allow the score to become negative.

answer.text: PROCEDURE UpdateScore(BYREF Score : INTEGER, Bonus : INTEGER)
Score ← Score + Bonus
Validation: IF Score > 100 THEN Score ← 100 / IF Score < 0 THEN Score ← 0, with ENDPROCEDURE

questions.explanation:
PROCEDURE UpdateScore(BYREF Score : INTEGER, Bonus : INTEGER)
    Score ← Score + Bonus
    IF Score > 100 THEN
        Score ← 100
    ENDIF
    IF Score < 0 THEN
        Score ← 0
    ENDIF
ENDPROCEDURE

questions.text: Why is passing a large array **by reference** usually preferable?

options.text: It copies every element, which is faster
It passes only the address, so it uses less memory and avoids copying time
It prevents the subroutine from reading the array

questions.explanation: Copying a large array is expensive; passing the address is efficient. The trade-off is that the subroutine can modify the original.

questions.text:
The procedure below is intended to swap two array elements but does not work.

```
PROCEDURE SwapItems(BYVAL P : INTEGER, BYVAL Q : INTEGER)
    DECLARE Temp : INTEGER
    Temp ← P
    P ← Q
    Q ← Temp
ENDPROCEDURE
```

State why it fails and write the corrected header.

answer.text: Both parameters are passed BYVAL, so only local copies are swapped — the calling variables are unchanged.
Corrected header: PROCEDURE SwapItems(BYREF P : INTEGER, BYREF Q : INTEGER)

questions.explanation: Swapping is the canonical example of needing BYREF.

questions.text: Describe the purpose of **registers** in the processor and explain why they are needed instead of just using RAM.

answer.text: Registers are small storage locations inside the CPU used to hold data, addresses and instructions currently in use.
They are much faster than RAM because they are on the CPU and accessed directly (no bus transfer delay).
Using registers reduces the number of slow memory accesses, speeding up the FDE cycle.

questions.explanation: Registers are the fastest storage in the memory hierarchy.
